title: How GPS knows where you are

sections.title: Clocks that run fast in orbit

narration: Say it's night, and you open a map.
A blue dot appears, right where you stand.
beats.visual_intent: A city at night from above; a phone screen lights with a map and a blue dot pulses into place.

grounding.claim: a viewer opening a map at night

narration: Your phone hasn't told anyone where it is.
So how does it know?
beats.visual_intent: Pull back from the phone up through the night sky to Earth in the dark field; the phone a single glowing point.

grounding.claim: the phone transmits nothing to GPS satellites

narration: The answer is overhead.
And it's all about time:
keeping it, measuring it, correcting it.
beats.visual_intent: Satellites fade in on their orbits around Earth; three small clock marks light one by one as each verb lands.

grounding.claim: GPS position rests on satellite time stamps and travel time

narration: It runs on two things you know:
satellites in orbit, and the speed of light.
beats.visual_intent: One satellite traced around its orbit; a beam of light streaks across the field beside it.

grounding.claim: signals travel at the speed of light

narration: About 24 GPS satellites, by design.
Each about 20,200 kilometres up,
circling every 12 hours or so.
beats.visual_intent: The constellation fills in: orbital rings tilt around Earth, satellites travelling along them; the altitude marked on one radius line.

grounding.claim: constellation designed around 24 satellites
about 20,200 km altitude, about 12 hour orbit

narration: Each carries atomic clocks,
and each one is broadcasting, all the time.
beats.visual_intent: Close on one satellite; a clock face on its body ticks; rings of signal pulse outward from it and from the others.

grounding.claim: satellites carry atomic clocks
continuous broadcast

narration: Every signal says two things.
Here is where I am.
And here is exactly when I sent this.
beats.visual_intent: One pulse carries two tags riding the wavefront: a position marker and a time stamp, each appearing on its words.

grounding.claim: signal carries the satellite's orbit data
signal carries the time of sending

narration: Your phone only listens.
Nothing goes up.
The satellites never learn where you are.
beats.visual_intent: Signals arrive at the phone on the ground; an arrow from the phone upward is drawn and fades out, nothing leaves it.

grounding.claim: receiver is passive

beats.misconception: the phone sends a signal up and the satellites track it

narration: A signal leaves, stamped with its sending time,
and heads for your phone.
beats.visual_intent: One satellite fires a single pulse with its time stamp; the pulse travels down toward the phone.

grounding.claim: signal stamped with time of sending

narration: It's a radio wave, moving at light speed:
about 300,000 kilometres a second.
beats.visual_intent: The pulse in flight, the speed label riding beside it.

grounding.claim: radio waves travel at about 300,000 km/s

narration: From straight overhead,
the trip takes about 0.07 seconds.
beats.visual_intent: A timer on the phone counts while the pulse completes its trip, stopping as it arrives.

grounding.claim: about 0.07 s from overhead

narration: Your phone takes the arrival time,
subtracts the sending time,
and multiplies by the speed of light.
beats.visual_intent: The two times sit on the phone; the arrival minus the sending gives travel time, which multiplies into a distance, each step on its word.

grounding.claim: distance from travel time times speed of light

narration: That gives a distance.
Not a direction: only a distance.
beats.visual_intent: A straight line from satellite to phone, labelled; a direction arrow is offered and struck out.

grounding.claim: ranging gives a distance only

narration: So the phone sits somewhere on a sphere
around that satellite, at exactly that range.
beats.visual_intent: The distance line sweeps around the satellite, drawing a full sphere (a circle in the flat picture) that grazes the Earth where the phone is.

grounding.claim: one distance places the receiver on a sphere

narration: Add a second satellite.
Where the two spheres meet, they trace a circle.
beats.visual_intent: A second satellite's sphere grows; where it crosses the first, a ring of overlap lights up.

grounding.claim: two spheres intersect in a circle

narration: A third sphere cuts that circle
at just two points.
beats.visual_intent: A third sphere grows and the ring collapses to two bright points.

grounding.claim: a third sphere narrows to two points

narration: One is usually far out in space.
The other, on the ground, is you.
In principle.
beats.visual_intent: One point drifts into the void and dims; the other sits on Earth's surface over the city and glows.

grounding.claim: in principle three satellites suffice; one point is far from Earth

beats.delivery: a beat of hesitation on 'in principle'

narration: Because all of this assumed
your phone knows the exact time.
It doesn't.
beats.visual_intent: The glowing point flickers; the frame cuts in to the phone and its clock.

grounding.claim: three suffice only with a perfect receiver clock

narration: Satellites have atomic clocks.
Your phone has a cheap quartz clock,
off by an amount it can't know.
beats.visual_intent: Two clocks side by side: the satellite's steady, the phone's visibly off its hand position.

grounding.claim: phone clock is cheap quartz, far less accurate

narration: And here, time is distance.
Light covers about 300 metres in a microsecond.
So a microsecond off is 300 metres off.
beats.visual_intent: A tiny tick of the clock unrolls into a long ruler across the city map, 300 metres long.

grounding.claim: 1 microsecond of error is about 300 m

narration: And the error is the same for every satellite.
Every sphere swells together,
and they stop meeting at one point.
beats.visual_intent: Back on the diagram: all three circles grow by the same amount and the single point breaks into a blurred patch with no common meeting.

grounding.claim: every distance is shifted by the same unknown amount

narration: Every distance is wrong by the same amount.
Before I show you:
what would fix it?
beats.visual_intent: The broken diagram holds still; the question appears beside it and the frame waits.

grounding.claim: shared clock error

narration: One more satellite.
A fourth sphere is one more measurement
than position alone needs.
beats.visual_intent: A fourth satellite rises over the horizon and its circle grows into the diagram.

grounding.claim: at least four satellites needed

narration: Four unknowns: east, north, height,
and the clock error.
The phone finds the one clock error
that makes all four spheres meet,
and its position comes with it.
beats.visual_intent: Four unknown tiles light as named; then all four circles shrink together by the same amount until they snap to one shared point, and the phone's clock hand jumps to the right time.

grounding.claim: four unknowns: three position, one clock error; fourth signal solves the clock

narration: So the phone's clock is handled.
But it all rests on the satellites' clocks.
Are they right?
beats.visual_intent: Pull back up from the phone to a satellite in orbit; its clock comes into focus.

grounding.claim: ranging uses the satellite's time stamp

recall.prompt: the time stamp that turned travel time into distance

narration: Satellites move fast.
Special relativity says a moving clock runs slow:
about 7 microseconds a day.
on_screen: speed: about 7 microseconds a day slower
beats.visual_intent: Two clocks side by side, ground and orbit; as the satellite speeds along its orbit, its clock falls behind.

grounding.claim: special relativity slows satellite clocks about 7 microseconds a day

beats.misconception: relativity is a curiosity with no practical effect

narration: But up there, gravity is weaker.
General relativity says that makes a clock run fast:
about 45 microseconds a day.
on_screen: gravity: about 45 microseconds a day faster
beats.visual_intent: The gravity well of Earth drawn shallowing with height; the orbit clock now races ahead of the ground clock.

grounding.claim: general relativity speeds satellite clocks about 45 microseconds a day

narration: Gravity wins.
A satellite clock gains about 38 microseconds a day.
on_screen: net: about 38 microseconds a day faster
beats.visual_intent: The two effects as opposing pushes on the clock, the larger winning; the net gain settles on the orbit clock.

grounding.claim: net gain about 38 microseconds a day

narration: At 300 metres a microsecond,
that's roughly 10 kilometres of error,
building up every day.
beats.visual_intent: Back on the city map: a day counter runs and the blue dot slides steadily away from the phone across the city.

grounding.claim: 1 microsecond about 300 m
uncorrected error builds roughly 10 km a day

narration: So the fix goes up with them.
Before launch, each clock is set slightly slow,
so in orbit it keeps ground time.
beats.visual_intent: The satellite's clock is adjusted on the ground, launched, and in orbit its hands fall into step with the ground clock; the blue dot slides back home.

grounding.claim: clock rate set lower before launch to compensate

narration: So, the chain.
Satellites broadcast where and when.
Travel time gives distance.
Spheres meet.
A fourth satellite fixes your phone's clock.
beats.visual_intent: The diagram returns and replays in brief: pulse, timer, circles meeting, fourth circle snapping them to one point, each on its words.

grounding.claim: broadcast of position and time
distance from travel time
spheres intersect
fourth satellite for the clock

narration: And the satellites' clocks were set for relativity
before they ever left the ground.
beats.visual_intent: The ground and orbit clocks tick together in step beside the replayed diagram.

grounding.claim: pre-launch clock offset

narration: Real life adds noise.
The air slows signals a little,
and buildings bounce them.
So the dot is an estimate.
beats.visual_intent: Descend to the city: a signal bends slightly through the air and another reflects off a tall building; the blue dot shows a soft halo of uncertainty.

grounding.claim: atmosphere and buildings add error; position is an estimate

narration: But each time it appears,
your phone has just solved a timing problem.
And the dot lands where you are.
beats.visual_intent: Back to the phone screen from the opening: the blue dot settles on the map; pull back to the night city and the satellites passing above.

grounding.claim: the position is found by timing
fourth satellite solves the clock
